analysis.one_liner: Creates a no-fault compensation program for firefighters sickened by PFAS, funded by a tax on PFAS makers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in March 2024 with zero cosponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a no-fault federal program paying firefighters with PFAS-linked illnesses — $250,000 base for cancer, $50,000 for other conditions, multiplied up to 4x by years of service — without requiring them to prove who hurt them or sue anyone. The money would come from a new PFAS Trust Fund financed by a 10% excise tax on PFAS products sold by manufacturers and a 10% tax on large PFAS litigation settlements. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never taken up; it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Firefighters with at least two years of service who develop PFAS-linked cancers or other covered conditions, plus their families in cases of death. The program would pay a base award of $250,000 for cancer and $50,000 for non-cancer conditions, multiplied by a service modifier of 1 to 4 based on years served, with decisions due within 120 days and appeal rights to the Court of Federal Claims [S2].

how_it_helps.text: A firefighter with 2+ years of service and a diagnosed PFAS-linked condition would qualify for compensation without having to prove negligence or sue; the program presumes the condition was caused by PFAS exposure during firefighting [S2].

The program is no-fault: claims are decided by the Secretary within 120 days, awards are $250,000 for cancer and $50,000 for other conditions times a service modifier up to 4x for 10+ years of service, and claimants can appeal to the Court of Federal Claims with de novo review [S2].

Covered conditions include cancers of the kidney, testicle, liver, prostate, bladder, pancreas, breast, colon, and ovary, plus thyroid disease and ulcerative colitis, with an advisory panel to add more conditions [S2].
Families of deceased firefighters (estate administrators or adult heirs) could claim, and compensation would be shielded from the decedent's creditors [S2].

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers, producers, and importers, who would pay a 10% excise tax on PFAS products they sell, and any company paying large PFAS litigation awards or settlements other than personal-injury claims, which would owe a 10% tax on the present value of the payment. Some of these costs would likely be passed to buyers of PFAS-containing products [S2].

drawbacks.text: The program assumes causation rather than proving it: for listed conditions, the Secretary must conclude the illness was caused by PFAS exposure during firefighting and cannot consider any defense, which means some awards may go to people whose illness had other causes [S2].

Funding could fall short: the bill requires payments to be prorated when the trust fund is deficient, with later supplementation plus 6% interest, which shows the drafters anticipated that the excise taxes might not cover all claims [S2].

The 10% tax on PFAS products would raise prices for goods containing PFAS, including firefighting gear, and a tax on litigation settlements could make it more expensive for companies to resolve PFAS contamination cases [S2].
Each claimant is limited to one cancer and one non-cancer condition, and only one claim per firefighter, so claimants with multiple serious illnesses could not stack awards [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For firefighters — a workforce with heavy, repeated exposure to PFAS in gear and foam — a no-fault program with fast, defined awards would remove the burden of suing deep-pocketed chemical companies individually. The funding is designed to be self-financing from the industry whose products caused the exposure, not from general taxpayers. The main design risks are that causation is presumed rather than proven, and that the dedicated taxes could underfund the promised awards, forcing prorated payments; the bill also caps attorneys' fees, which protects claimants' awards but could shrink access to legal help. The bill never advanced far enough for any of this to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee never took it up after referral, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Booker introduced the bill on March 21, 2024; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S4].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and companies facing PFAS litigation are better off, because the 10% excise taxes that would have funded firefighter compensation never took effect. Firefighters with PFAS-linked illnesses gained nothing and remain reliant on lawsuits or workers' compensation systems.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Firefighter PFAS Injury Compensation Act of 2024 and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it expired at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition — just a single Democratic sponsor and committee inaction.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed a 10% excise tax on PFAS products they sell and a 10% tax on the present value of most PFAS litigation awards or settlements they pay, with the proceeds funding firefighter compensation. The bill's death leaves them paying neither tax.
A 10% tax on qualifying PFAS litigation awards (other than personal-injury claims) would have added cost to settlements over contamination and cleanup. It never took effect.
Firefighters would gain a guaranteed no-fault payment path for PFAS-linked cancer and other conditions, replacing the uncertainty of litigation. The bill never advanced, so no benefit was delivered.
